what: Stewart platform / Gough–Stewart hexapod. Six independently powered small linear actuators connect a free-standing Technic base to a raised open platform. Small stock towballs at both ends let each leg change direction. The six leg lengths jointly determine three translations and three rotations of the plate. Six colours identify physical legs A–F; their motor ports are F, B, D, A, E, C respectively.
try: Open Examples and choose Atlas Six, then open the model with its program. The model, Code and Blocks load together. Press Reset, then Run. Reset again before repeating or after manual movement; keep manual overrides off during the experiment.

Watch the finite 27-stage sequence: separate positive and negative translations, separate rotations, a small combined pose, and return home. Each excursion returns to the saved datum before the next one. The targets are ±2 mm along each LDraw axis, ±1.5° about X and Z, and ±1.2° about vertical Y; +Y points downward.
Look at two different-coloured legs while the plate moves vertically. Compare their screw turns. Their angles and saved extensions differ, so equal plate motion does not imply equal motor rotation.

Predict which lengths must change for a rotation about vertical Y. Then observe the yaw stages and compare the planned motor targets with the observed platform pose. All six commands begin concurrently; each motor finishes its own bounded move, and the stage waits for all six.

Before another run, use Pause → Reset → Run. Keep manual overrides off and do not erase the encoder datum separately. After returning home, all motors hold for one settling second before completion sets completed=1, failed=0 and stage=28. The motors continue holding afterward.
why: For a proposed plate pose, rotate each upper anchor about the declared platform origin, translate it, and measure its distance from the corresponding base anchor. Here the two ball centres are offset sideways by 30 LDU from one another relative to the actuator axis. Therefore the piston extension is the square root of ball distance squared minus 30 squared, less the 120-LDU axial body offset. Subtract the saved extension and divide by the screw lead to obtain motor turns. The native solver must still produce and retain the requested plate pose under its actual weight; the inverse equation supplies motor inputs, not observed motion.
matters: Parallel mechanisms share a load among several simultaneous chains. A Stewart-type platform exposes a useful distinction between inverse kinematics, which computes actuator lengths for a chosen pose, and forward motion, which must emerge from the assembled constraints. Geometry, singularity margin, socket articulation and finite screw stroke all limit the useful workspace.
question: If every motor turns forward by exactly the same angle, must this asymmetric platform translate vertically without rotating?
answer: No. Equal motor turns add equal piston extension, but the six struts have different saved lengths and directions. Their projections onto a vertical displacement differ. Compute all six target extensions from the same desired platform pose, then drive the corresponding hub ports. Equal turns alone do not impose a pure translation.
further: A small actuator has a native physical slider range of 0–60 LDU (24 mm). The demonstration stays inside a smaller measured range. The software route is not a physical stop, and the separate per-axis limits do not authorize their simultaneous combination.

The selected stock ball/socket geometry is checked against a conservative 25° stem-angle cap. Native ball joints can rotate without a rim limit, so passing physics alone would miss a neck-to-socket collision. Actual body recordings and stock-mesh clearance are checked separately.

The leg assemblies can roll passively around the line between their end balls. Their motors hang toward the stable gravity orientation; no hidden antiroll weld is added. Their observed roll and cold settling must remain inside the checked socket envelope.

Each motor stator is physically pinned to its actuator body. A 3L axle and open-bore 6538a joiner turn the spindle. A joiner with an internal axle stop is not an interchangeable substitute at this engagement depth.
The chassis is free on the floor. Three non-collinear points on actual plate beams measure the six-axis pose relative to the observed hub. Targets do not supply those measured positions.

The historical Stewart paper describes a six-motor platform concept: D. Stewart, A Platform with Six Degrees of Freedom (1965), https://doi.org/10.1243/PIME_PROC_1965_180_029_02. This stock-part layout, code and lessons are original work. Physical assembly, flexible cable retention and hardware accuracy remain untested.
formula: LDraw units: 1 LDU=0.4 mm, +Y downward. Let b_i be base anchor, p_i saved upper anchor, o=[0,-140,0], t the commanded translation and R=Rz Ry Rx. q_i=o+t+R(p_i-o); e_i=sqrt(||q_i-b_i||^2-30^2)-120; theta_i=360(e_i-e_i0)/3.0147 degrees. Physical legs A,B,C,D,E,F map to hub ports F,B,D,A,E,C. These equations are target inputs, not measured outputs.
